blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: High up in the sky there is a house. It is not on a hill. It is not on a street. It floats. The house is called the space station. People live inside it. They eat and sleep and work up there. Nothing sits still in the space station. Cups float. Spoons float. The people float too. The space station goes all the way around the Earth while you eat your lunch.

blocks.prompt: A Home in the Sky
blocks.text: The space station is a home in the sky. It flies about 250 miles above your head. That is far above the clouds, and much higher than any airplane can go. Inside, there is no up and no down. Astronauts push off a wall with one finger and glide across the room. They sleep in bags tied to the wall, so they do not drift away in the night. The space station moves very fast. It goes all the way around the Earth in about ninety minutes. That means the astronauts watch the sun come up sixteen times every day.

blocks.prompt: Built in the Sky, One Piece at a Time
blocks.text: The International Space Station is the biggest thing people have ever built off the Earth. It is about as long as a football field, and it weighs almost a million pounds. It flies roughly 250 miles up, circling the planet once every ninety minutes. Nobody carried it up in one piece. No rocket is big enough. So engineers built it like a model kit. They launched one piece at a time, over more than forty flights, and astronauts bolted the pieces together while floating outside in their suits. People have lived on board without a single break since November 2000. Somebody has been up there every day since then, including your last birthday, including today. Living there takes practice. Water does not pour, it clumps into wobbling balls. Salt and pepper come as liquids, because loose grains would drift off and land in somebody's eye. Astronauts strap into a treadmill for two hours a day, because muscles and bones get lazy when nothing has any weight.

notes: Gravity up there is still about 90 percent as strong

blocks.prompt: Why the Space Station Does Not Fall Down
blocks.text: Ask most people why astronauts float on the space station and they will tell you there is no gravity up there. That answer is wrong, and the truth is much better. At 250 miles up, Earth's gravity is still about ninety percent as strong as it is in your kitchen. The station is absolutely being pulled down. It is falling right now, as you read this. The reason it never lands is that it is also moving sideways at about 17,500 miles per hour. It falls, the ground curves away beneath it, and it misses. It has been missing the Earth for more than twenty five years. That is all an orbit is: falling forever, and missing. Everything inside falls at exactly the same rate, which is why an astronaut, her pencil, and her water bottle all hang in the air together as though weight had been switched off. Scientists call this microgravity, not zero gravity. Falling forever creates problems nobody expected. Hot air does not rise, so a candle burns as a dim blue ball instead of a teardrop. Sweat does not drip, it spreads across skin in a clinging film. Bones lose about one percent of their mass every month, so crews exercise two hours a day, strapped down so they do not launch themselves into the ceiling. Water is the hardest problem of all. Hauling it up by rocket costs a fortune, so the station recycles nearly everything it can, including sweat, the moisture in the crew's breath, and urine. The recovery system captures about ninety eight percent of it. Astronauts have a saying about the coffee up there: yesterday's coffee becomes today's coffee.

5.title: The House That Never Stops Falling

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Assembled in orbit between 1998 and 2011
Five space agencies: USA, Russia, Europe, Japan, Canada
About 356 feet across, roughly 925,000 pounds
Oxygen made by splitting water with electricity
Continuously crewed since November 2, 2000
Planned to be steered down into the Pacific around 2030

blocks.prompt: A Machine Built by Rivals
blocks.text: In 1975, an American Apollo capsule docked with a Soviet Soyuz in orbit, and the two commanders shook hands through the open hatch. On the ground, their countries were aiming nuclear weapons at each other. Twenty three years later, those same two nations began bolting a house together in the sky. The International Space Station was assembled in orbit between 1998 and 2011, from modules built in the United States, Russia, Japan, Europe, and Canada. No single rocket could lift it. Each piece flew up separately, and astronauts joined them together on spacewalks, working in pressurized suits with the planet turning below their boots. Finished, the station spans about 356 feet, roughly the length of a football field, and weighs around 925,000 pounds. It is the most expensive object ever built. Its parts were designed on different continents, in different languages, and they had to fit together on the first try, in vacuum, at 17,500 miles per hour. The station makes its own air. Electricity from its solar arrays splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, and the crew breathes the oxygen. Carbon dioxide is scrubbed back out of the cabin before it can build up to a dangerous level. Water is reclaimed from sweat, from the humidity the crew exhales, and from urine, at a recovery rate near ninety eight percent. Almost nothing is thrown away, because anything thrown away must be replaced by a rocket. Crews have lived on board continuously since November 2, 2000. Not one day since then has passed with every human being on Earth. More than 280 people from over twenty countries have visited, and thousands of experiments have run on board, from growing lettuce in a box to burning flames that make no smoke. The station will not last forever. Metal fatigues, seals leak, and even at 250 miles up there are thin traces of atmosphere dragging it slowly downward, so engines must shove it back up again and again. Around 2030, the agencies plan to steer the whole structure down into a remote stretch of the South Pacific, where it will break apart and burn. The most complicated thing our species has ever assembled will end as a streak of light over empty ocean, watched by almost nobody.

6.title: The House That Never Stops Falling
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The House That Never Stops Falling

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: 1993: the USA and Russia agree to build it together
US segment supplied power, Russian segment supplied propulsion
42 assembly flights from two continents, 1998 to 2011
925,000 pounds, 356 feet, 17,500 miles per hour
Water recovery near 98 percent, oxygen split from water
Deorbit planned around 2030 into the South Pacific

blocks.prompt: Falling Forever: The Machine Built by Enemies
blocks.text: Nothing about the International Space Station should have worked. Consider the political problem first. The station's two largest partners, the United States and Russia, spent forty years of the twentieth century preparing to destroy one another. In 1993, with the Soviet Union barely two years dead, their space agencies agreed to build a laboratory together in orbit. Neither could easily walk away afterward, because the design made them dependent on each other. For years the American segment supplied most of the electrical power, while the Russian segment supplied the engines that kept the whole structure from sinking out of the sky. Each half was useless alone. That was not an accident of engineering. It was a decision. Now consider the physical problem. The station weighs around 925,000 pounds and stretches about 356 feet, the length of a football field. No rocket that has ever flown could lift it. So it was not lifted. It was mailed, piece by piece, across more than forty launches from two continents between 1998 and 2011, and assembled by astronauts in pressurized suits traveling at 17,500 miles per hour, with the Earth rolling past beneath their boots every ninety minutes. Modules machined in Russia, Japan, Italy, and the United States met for the first time in vacuum, at speed, and had to mate on the first attempt. There was no workshop, no second try, no way to send a part back. The station survives on closed loops. Solar arrays feed electricity to a system that splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, and the crew breathes the oxygen. Scrubbers pull carbon dioxide back out of the cabin air before it reaches a dangerous level. The water recovery system reclaims sweat, exhaled humidity, and urine, returning roughly ninety eight percent of it to the drinking supply. This is not thrift for its own sake. Every pound that cannot be recycled must be flown up on a rocket, and rockets are the most expensive delivery service ever devised. Scarcity, not virtue, made the station the most efficient recycler humans have ever operated. And the whole arrangement is falling. This is the part most people get wrong. Gravity at that altitude is still roughly ninety percent as strong as it is at your kitchen table. The station is pulled toward the ground constantly, and constantly fails to arrive, because it is also traveling sideways fast enough that the planet curves away beneath it. An orbit is not an escape from gravity. It is a permanent, accurate miss. Everything inside falls at the same rate as the walls, which is why a wrench, a crumb, and a scientist all hang in the air together. Since November 2, 2000, there has not been a single day when every living human was on Earth. That may be the station's real achievement, and it is not a scientific one. Thousands of experiments have run on board, and some of them matter, but no discovery from those laboratories has changed the world the way the plain existence of the thing has. It is proof that the countries with the deepest reasons to distrust each other can keep a shared machine alive for a quarter of a century, in a place where a mistake by any of them kills all of them. Around 2030, it comes down. Thin traces of atmosphere drag at it, metal fatigues, seals age, and the plan is to fire engines and steer the entire structure into an empty stretch of the South Pacific, where it will break apart and burn. The most complex object our species has ever built will end as a bright streak over open water. The day after it falls, the sky above us will be empty of people for the first time in thirty years.
